summary:
Castilla y León stands under Spain's national framework. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition of the acquired gender is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Other operative provisions of the same statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Castilla y León, in contrast to the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510 (one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months) derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Regional legislation is being built on top of the national floor. The PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León on 20 December 2024, framed as an end to the "sexilio", the out-migration of LGBTI people from the region, with group leader Tudanca urging the fastest possible processing. On 11 June 2025 the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the bill, which runs to 76 articles, into consideration after the PP abstained and Vox opposed; the bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands, and advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.
tangentialFactors:
Spain's self-declaration model is grouped with Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay, all of which use administrative routes rather than medical gatekeeping for legal gender change. The United Kingdom is moving in the opposite direction on single-sex spaces, applying biological-sex lines with restrictions decided case by case rather than as a blanket ban, which matters for a trans visitor comparing the two.

The 2016 survey of 23 countries that placed Spain at the top of the group on trans support predates Ley 4/2023 by seven years and should be read as a baseline rather than a current measurement.

Regional legislative activity in Castilla y León is contested rather than settled: the equality bill drew PP abstention and Vox opposition when taken into consideration, and LGBTI advocates have publicly warned that committee stage could stall it.
localsOnly:
Residents of Castilla y León obtain legal gender recognition through the national Civil Registry under Article 43 of Ley 4/2023, without a diagnosis or a treatment period; the regional administration does not run a separate procedure. Consent rules for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition of acquired gender from age 12 under conditions, apply to residents on the same national terms.

The PSOE-sponsored regional equality bill, registered on 20 December 2024 and taken into consideration on 11 June 2025, runs to 76 articles and was drafted in answer to long-standing demands from regional LGBTI+ collectives. Its stated aim includes ending the "sexilio", the departure of LGBTI people from Castilla y León for other regions, and the group leader Tudanca pressed for the fastest possible processing.

Anti-discrimination protections in healthcare, employment and housing, the ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples and the expanded assisted reproduction rules all reach residents of Castilla y León through the national statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The final passage of the Castilla y León equality bill is unresolved in the sources: they record registration in December 2024 and the vote to take it into consideration in June 2025, but no committee outcome, floor vote or entry into force. Whether the bill has since been adopted, amended or dropped is not sourced here.

No enforcement data specific to Castilla y León is available in this inventory. The two documented applications of the gender-identity aggravation, in Vigo in July 2026 and in Valencia in January 2026, both arise outside the region and are cited as evidence that the aggravating circumstance is applied in practice, not as a measure of regional policing or judicial practice.

Whether Castilla y León has issued regional implementing regulations, service guidance or facility-access instructions under Ley 4/2023 is not sourced. The comparative ranking from the 2016 survey is a dated baseline and no post-2023 equivalent survey appears in the inventory.
